nodes.name: Euclidean X-ray transform

nodes.name: Vanishing of functions with empty analytic wavefront set
nodes.statement: For if an unknown function $f$ supported in $\Omega$ satisfies $WF_{A}(f) \cap T^{*}\Omega = \emptyset$, then $f$ must be entire and compactly supported, and hence must vanish identically.
assumptions: an unknown function $f$ supported in $\Omega$ satisfies $WF_{A}(f) \cap T^{*}\Omega = \emptyset$

nodes.statement_short: Partial Cauchy data: Dirichlet traces on $\Gamma_D$ and Neumann traces on $\Gamma_N$ of solutions of $(-\Delta+q)u=0$.

nodes.statement: The authors then consider the case when $\Omega$ is a Riemannian manifold $(M,g) \Subset (\mathbb{R} \times \widetilde{M}_{0}, g)$ where $g = c(e \oplus g_{0})$, $(\widetilde{M}_{0}, g_{0})$ is some compact $(n-1)$-dimensional simple manifold with boundary, and $e$ is the euclidean metric on the real line.

Boundary decomposition by limiting Carleman weight

nodes.statement_short: Equal partial Cauchy data imply vanishing exponentially weighted broken ray integrals of the Fourier-transformed potential difference.
assumptions: let $\Gamma_{i} \subset \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}}$ such that there exists a nonempty open subset $E$ of $\partial M_{0}$, and suppose $\Gamma_{D} = \Gamma_{N} = \Gamma$ for some neighborhood $\Gamma$ in $\partial M$ of the set $\overline{\partial M_{+} \cup \partial M_{-} \cup \Gamma_{a}}$ for $\Gamma_{a} = \partial M_{\mathrm{tan}} \setminus \Gamma_{i}$

nodes.statement: It is the author's belief, however, that the results herein are generalizable to at least to convex domains in $\rn{n}$ with piecewise flat reflective boundaries.
conclusions: the results herein are generalizable to at least to convex domains in $\rn{n}$ with piecewise flat reflective boundaries

nodes.name: Outgoing and ingoing unit vectors $\Gamma_{\pm}$
nodes.statement: Let $\Omega$ be a smooth bounded domain in $\rn{n}$ and define $\Gamma_{\pm} = \{(x,\theta) \in \partial \Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1} \, | \, \pm \nu(x) \cdot \theta >0\}$ as the set of outgoing and ingoing unit vectors on $\partial \Omega$, respectively. Here $\nu(x)$ is the outward unit normal vector to $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Boundary vectors over $E$, $\Gamma_{\pm}(E)$
Definition of $\Gamma_{\pm}(E)$
nodes.statement: \Gamma_{\pm}(E) := \{(x,\theta) \in S\Omega \, | \, x \in E, \pm \theta \cdot \nu(x) > 0\}.

nodes.name: Smooth attenuation vanishing near the boundary
nodes.statement: Assume that $\sigma \in C^{\infty}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$ and vanishes near $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Regular broken ray
differentia: its associated tangent vector field $(\gamma_{x,\theta}(t), \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta}(t))$ intersects $\Gamma_{-}(E)$
it consists of finitely many straight line segments $\gamma_{x,\theta,1}, \gamma_{x,\theta,2}, \ldots, \gamma_{x,\theta,N}$ before hitting $E$ again
it obeys the geometrical optics reflection law
nodes.statement_short: A unit-speed curve from $\Gamma_-(E)$, finitely many segments, avoiding $\partial E$, obeying optical reflection.

nodes.name: Geometrical optics reflection law
nodes.statement: \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j+1}(0) = \dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j}) - 2\left\langle \nu(\gamma_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j})),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j}) \right\rangle \nu(\gamma_{x,\theta,j}(L_{j})), \,1 \leq j \leq N.

nodes.name: Billiard map $T$
nodes.statement: We use the notation $T:\Gamma_{-} \to \Gamma_{-}$ to denote the billiard map mapping a vector $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}$ to $(x',\theta') \in \Gamma_{-}$, where $x'$ is the intersection point of the geodesic $\gamma_{x,\theta}$ with $\partial \Omega$, and $\theta'$ is the reflected direction.

nodes.name: Projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$
nodes.statement: We use the maps $\pi_{1},\pi_{2}$ to denote the projections $\Gamma_{-} \to \partial \Omega$ and $\Gamma_{-} \to \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Travel times $\tau_{\pm}$ and reflection count $N(x,\theta)$
nodes.statement: Also $\tau_{\pm}(x,\theta) = \min \{ t \geq 0 \, | \, x + t\theta \in \partial \Omega\}$ are the positive and negative travel times from a given unit tangent vector $(x,\theta) \in S\Omega$, and $N(x,\theta)$ for $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ will denote the number of reflections of the given trajectory before intersecting $E$.

nodes.name: Extension $g^{\#}$ of boundary functions
nodes.statement: We use the notation $g^{\#}(x,\theta) := g(x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta, \theta)$ to denote the extension of a function $g$ on $\Gamma_{-}$ to $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Unattenuated broken ray transform $I_{0,E}$
nodes.statement_short: $I_{0,E}f$ sums the line integrals of $f$ over all segments of the broken ray.

nodes.name: Unattenuated broken ray transform formula
nodes.statement: I_{0, E}f(\gamma_{x,\theta}) = I_{0, E}f(x,\theta) := \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} f(\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt.
nodes.label: forwardoperator

nodes.name: Reflection points and directions $z_j,\theta_j$
Definition of $(z_j,\theta_j)$
nodes.statement: (z_{j}(x,\theta),\theta_{j}(x,\theta)) = T^{j}(x+\tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta,\theta), \quad (x,\theta) \in S\Omega.
nodes.label: eq:zjthetaj

nodes.name: Cutoff operator $\alpha I_{0,E}$
nodes.statement: Thus, we will instead consider the cutoff operator $\alpha I_{0, E}$, where $\alpha:\Gamma_{-}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth cutoff function supported on some subset of broken rays that have at most $N_{max} \geq 0$ reflections.

nodes.name: Reflections at corners of the square
nodes.statement: Although general polyhedral domains lack obvious reflection rules at the corners (some authors ignore such trajectories and some define them in terms of limits of regular trajectories, e.g. \cite{eskin}), the special symmetrical nature of the square does give an unambiguous rule for such reflections. But one still runs into the problem that the composite functions $z_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta)$ are not real analytic for $(x,\theta)$ associated with a corner point. One simple, albeit more restrictive route, is to assume that the subset $E$ also includes a small neighborhood of each corner. In that case, all broken rays with corner points are just ballistic X-rays. More generally, one can cut out the rays with corner points from the measurement operator. However, if one assumes the attenuation coefficient to vanish in a neighborhood of the boundary, it is still possible to treat rays with corners as we will discuss later.
nodes.statement_short: Square corners have an unambiguous reflection rule, but $z_j,\theta_j$ are not analytic there; options: include corners in $E$, cut them out, or treat them later.

nodes.name: Reflection count is piecewise constant
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that $N(x,\theta)$ is piecewise constant, which leads to the unfortunate fact that $I_{0, E}$ in general does not preserve the smoothness of a function.
conclusions: $N(x,\theta)$ is piecewise constant

nodes.name: Analytic wavefront set notation
nodes.statement: From hereon we use the notation $\mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$ to denote the analytic wavefront set of $f$.

nodes.name: Path unfolding
nodes.statement: The main idea we use in order to apply microlocal analytic techniques to the operator is a well-known method of billiards called path unfolding.

nodes.name: Unfolded domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$
nodes.statement: Essentially, we can unfold any broken ray in $\Omega$ into a straight line on a different domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ defined by reflecting $\Omega$ across each of its edges repeatedly to obtain a tiling of $\rn{2}$.

nodes.name: Reflected extension $\widetilde{f}$
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can extend $f$ to a function $\widetilde{f}$ on $\widetilde{\Omega}$ by reflection across $\partial \Omega$.

nodes.name: Reflection signature
nodes.statement: We will use indices $(l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}$ to denote how many horizontal and vertical reflections a given broken ray undergoes on the unfolded domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ before returning to the set $E$. We call this the \textit{reflection signature} of a path.
nodes.statement_short: The reflection signature $(l_1,l_2)$ counts horizontal and vertical reflections of an unfolded broken ray.

nodes.name: Reflection maps $R_{l_1,l_2}$
Reflected angle $S_{l_1,l_2}$
Formula for $\widetilde{f}$
Reflected extension of $f$
nodes.statement:
\widetilde{f}(x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
f(R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(x)) & \textrm{ if }x \in [l_{1},l_{1}+1] \times [l_{2},l_{2}+1]\\
& (l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2},
\end{array}\right.

conclusions: one can also write $I_{0,E}f$ in the form

nodes.name: Unfolded integral form of $I_{0,E}f$
nodes.statement: I_{0, E}f(x,\theta) = \int_{0}^{L(\gamma_{x,\theta})}\widetilde{f}(x+t\theta)\,dt,

nodes.name: Extension of $\alpha I_{0,E}$ to distributions
nodes.statement_short: Fixing a common length $L$ on a beam of equal signature, duality makes $\alpha I_{0,E}f$ well defined for $f\in\mathcal{E}'(\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Duality formula for $\alpha I_{0,E}$
nodes.statement: \langle \alpha I_{0,E}f, \phi \rangle = \left\langle \widetilde{f}, \int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\alpha^{\#}(\cdot, \theta)\phi^{\#}(\cdot, \theta)\,d\theta \right \rangle,

nodes.name: Visible set $\mathcal{M}$
nodes.statement_short: Points $x$ all of whose conormal directions are covered by regular broken rays with at most $N_{max}$ reflections.

nodes.name: Visible set formula
nodes.statement:
\mathcal{M} & := \{x \in \Omega \, | \, \forall \xi \in \mathbb{S}^{1}, (x,\xi) \in N^{*}\gamma \textrm{ for some regular broken ray $\gamma$}\\
& \hspace{7cm} \textrm{ with $N(\gamma) \leq N_{max}$}\}. \notag

nodes.name: Examples of the visible set
nodes.statement:
One simple example of what $\mathcal{M}$ looks like is the case when $E$ contains two adjacent edges of the square $\Omega = (0,1)^2$. Then $\mathcal{M} = \Omega$.

Similarly, if $\Omega = \{x \in \rn{n} \, | \, |x| \leq 1 \}$, then for $E$ containing a hemisphere we have $\mathcal{M} = \Omega$.

In general, if $E = \bigcup_{j}E_{j}$ is a union of connected open subsets $E_{j}$ of the boundary, then we always have $\bigcup_{j} \mathrm{ch}(E_{j})\subset \mathcal{M}$, where $\mathrm{ch}$ denotes the closed convex hull. However, this is the part of $\mathcal{M}$ that is attributed to only ballistic (unreflected) X-rays.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{M}=\Omega$ if $E$ has two adjacent edges of the square, or a hemisphere of the ball; convex hulls of components of $E$ always lie in $\mathcal{M}$.

nodes.name: Injectivity of the broken ray transform on the square
nodes.statement:
Let $E \subset \partial \Omega$ be open, let $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be the corresponding visible set,
and let $K \Subset \mathcal{M}$. Then $I_{0, E}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$.
assumptions: $E \subset \partial \Omega$ be open
$N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$
$\mathcal{M}$ be the corresponding visible set
$K \Subset \mathcal{M}$
conclusions: $I_{0, E}$ is injective on $L^{2}(K)$
nodes.label: thm:injectivesquare

nodes.name: Attenuated broken ray transform $I_{\sigma,E}$
nodes.statement:
The broken ray transform with respect to $E\subset \partial \Omega$ and with attenuation $\sigma$, denoted by $I_{\sigma, E}:L^{2}(\Omega) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$, is defined as
\begin{align}
& \quad I_{\sigma, E}f(\gamma_{x,\theta}) = I_{\sigma, E}f(x,\theta) \notag \\
& := \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \exp\left( - \sum_{m=0}^{j-1}\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(\pi_{1} \circ T^{m}(x,\theta) + \tau \pi_{2}\circ T^{m}(x,\theta), \pi_{2} \circ T^{m}(x,\theta))\,d\tau\right) \notag\\
& \qquad \cdot \exp\left(-\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(\pi_{1}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + (t-\tau)\pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta), \pi_{2} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) )\,d\tau\right) \notag \\
& \qquad \cdot f(\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \\
& = \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \left[w_{j}f\right](\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta), \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \notag\\
& = \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \left[w_{j}f\right](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t \theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \notag
\end{align}
for all regular broken rays $\gamma_{x,\theta}$. The functions $z_{j}, \theta_{j}$ are defined in (\ref{eq:zjthetaj}).
nodes.statement_short: $I_{\sigma,E}f$ sums attenuated line integrals of $f$ over the segments of each broken ray.

nodes.name: Attenuated broken ray transform formula
nodes.statement:
& \quad I_{\sigma, E}f(\gamma_{x,\theta}) = I_{\sigma, E}f(x,\theta) \notag \\
& := \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \exp\left( - \sum_{m=0}^{j-1}\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(\pi_{1} \circ T^{m}(x,\theta) + \tau \pi_{2}\circ T^{m}(x,\theta), \pi_{2} \circ T^{m}(x,\theta))\,d\tau\right) \notag\\
& \qquad \cdot \exp\left(-\int_{\rn{+}}\sigma(\pi_{1}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + (t-\tau)\pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta), \pi_{2} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) )\,d\tau\right) \notag \\
& \qquad \cdot f(\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \\
& = \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \left[w_{j}f\right](\pi_{1} \circ T^{j}(x,\theta) + t \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta), \pi_{2}\circ T^{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \notag\\
& = \sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\int_{\rn{+}} \left[w_{j}f\right](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t \theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt. \notag
nodes.label: forwardoperator

nodes.name: Weight functions $w_j$
nodes.statement_short: $w_j$ is the exponential attenuation accumulated along the previous $j$ segments and the current one.

nodes.name: Smoothness of the weights $w_j$
nodes.statement: It is important to note that because $\sigma$ vanishes near $\partial \Omega$, the weight functions $w_{j}$ are smooth.
assumptions: $\sigma$ vanishes near $\partial \Omega$
conclusions: the weight functions $w_{j}$ are smooth

nodes.name: Proof of smoothness of $w_j$
nodes.statement: The reason is that we can circumscribe $\Omega$ with the ball $B = B\left( \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \right), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)$ and then replace $z_{m-j}(y,\eta) = \pi_{1} \circ T^{m-j}(y+ \tau_{-}(y,\eta)\eta,\eta)$ with the last point of $\partial B$ that intersects the line $z_{m-j}(y,\eta) + t\theta_{m-j}(y,\eta)$ for $t \leq 0$. This point is smoothly dependent on $(y,\eta) \in \Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace boundary hitting points by intersections with the circumscribed ball, which depend smoothly on $(y,\eta)$.

nodes.name: Reflected extension $\widetilde{\sigma}$
Reflected extension of $\sigma$
nodes.statement:
\widetilde{\sigma}(x,\theta) = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\sigma( R_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(x), S_{l_{1},l_{2}}^{-1}(\theta)) & \textrm{ for }x \in [l_{1},l_{1}+1] \times [l_{2},l_{2}+1],\\
&  \quad (l_{1},l_{2}) \in \mathbb{Z}^{2}.
\end{array}\right.

nodes.name: Unfolded weight $\widetilde{w}$
nodes.statement: Then $\widetilde{w}(x,\theta) := \exp\left( -\int_{0}^{L(\gamma_{x,-\theta})}\widetilde{\sigma}(x-\tau\theta,\theta)\,d\tau\right)$ is the associated weight for $(x,\theta) \in \widetilde{\Omega} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$.

nodes.name: Half broken ray length $L(\gamma_{x,-\theta})$
nodes.statement: We've used the notation $L(\gamma_{x,-\theta})$ to mean the length of the half broken ray with initial condition $(x,-\theta)$ before hitting some copy of $E$ in $\widetilde{\Omega}$.

nodes.name: Non-analyticity of the unfolded attenuation
nodes.statement: Obviously, $\sigma \equiv 0$ implies that $w \equiv 1$, which is analytic. However, for general $\sigma$ that are analytic on $\Omega$, it is not generally true that $\widetilde{\sigma}$ is analytic. In fact, it is easy to see that $\widetilde{\sigma}$ has symmetries somewhat like that of a doubly periodic function, which if analytic would necessarily be constant (the Weierstrass $\wp$-function is doubly periodic but has poles). This is the reason why we start with the case that the weight function is identically $1$ (equivalently $\sigma = 0$) and then prove stability for $C^{2}$ perturbations of $\sigma$ that remain $0$ in a neighborhood of $\partial \Omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Unfolded $\widetilde\sigma$ is doubly-periodic-like, so not analytic unless constant; hence start from $\sigma=0$ and perturb.

nodes.name: Boundedness of the cutoff broken ray transform
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Gamma_{-})$ and suppose all regular broken rays in $\mathrm{supp}(\alpha)$ have $\leq N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$ reflections. Then $I_{\sigma, E}:L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1}) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ is bounded.
assumptions: $\alpha \in C_{0}^{\infty}(\Gamma_{-})$
suppose all regular broken rays in $\mathrm{supp}(\alpha)$ have $\leq N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$ reflections
conclusions: $I_{\sigma, E}:L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1}) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-}, d\Sigma)$ is bounded

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement:
First we recall an identity from \cite{inversesource} which asserts that for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$, we have
\begin{equation*}
\int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta.
\end{equation*}
Now observe that
\begin{align*}
\| \alpha I_{\sigma, E} f(x,\theta) \|_{L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})}^{2} & \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} |\alpha(x,\theta)|^{2}\sum_{j=0}^{N(x,\theta)}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} [w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\
&\leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}}\left| \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} \chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}(t)[w_{j} f](z_{j}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j}(x,\theta), \theta_{j}(x,\theta))\,dt \right|^{2} \, d\Sigma\\
& \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \|\chi_{[0,\tau_{+}(z_{j},\theta_{j})]}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\|[w_{j}f](z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\
& \leq 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})}^{2}\,d\Sigma\\
& = 2 \int_{\Gamma_{-}} \sum_{j=0}^{N_{max}} \mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(z_{j}+t\theta_{j},\theta_{j})|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\
& = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\int_{\Gamma_{-}} \int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}|f(x+t\theta,\theta)|^{2}\,dt\,d\Sigma\\
& = 2 (N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1})}^{2}.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz on each segment plus Santalo's formula; the bound $N_{max}$ gives the constant $2(N_{max}+1)\mathrm{diam}(\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Santalo-type integration identity
assumptions: for any function $f \in L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{S}^{n-1})$
conclusions: \int_{\Gamma_{-}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}} f(x+t\theta, \theta)\,dt\,d\Sigma = \int_{\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(x,\theta)\,dx\,d\theta.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating line integrals over $\Gamma_-$ with measure $d\Sigma$ equals integration over $\Omega\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Localizing cutoffs $\alpha_k$
nodes.statement: Fix a positive $N_{max} \in \mathbb{N}$. For each regular broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with $N(x_{0},\theta_{0}) \leq N_{max}$, let $(l_{1},l_{2})$ be it's reflection signature on $\widetilde{\Omega}$. If $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ has no corner points, then find a maximal connected neighborhood $U \subset \Gamma_{-}(E)$ containing $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ such that all broken rays with initial data in $U$ are regular, have no corner points, and have the same reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$ (See Figure \ref{fig:beam}). In particular, $U$ itself contains no corner points. We then choose a smooth cutoff function $\alpha_{k}$ on $\Gamma_{-}$ that is equal to $1$ on a compact subset of $U$ and vanishes outside of $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Around a corner-free regular broken ray take a maximal neighborhood $U$ of rays with the same signature and a smooth cutoff $\alpha_k$ supported in $U$.

nodes.name: Cutoff at a corner starting point
nodes.statement: If $x_{0}$ is a corner point, then we consider all directed lines $\mathcal{L} = \{(x+t\theta,\theta) \, | \, t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ for $(x,\theta)$ in some neighborhood of $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ such that $N(x,\theta)$ is constant. Then take the intersection of $\mathcal{L}$ with the ball $B = \left( \left( \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right), \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)$ of radius $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ whose boundary $\partial B$ circumscribes $\Omega$. We then define a smooth function $\alpha$ on $\partial B \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ supported in $\partial B \times \mathbb{S}^{1} \cap \mathcal{L}$. We may then extend $\alpha$ to $\rn{2} \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$ to be constant on all directed lines $(x+t\theta, \theta)$. Its restriction to $\Gamma_{-}(\partial \Omega)$ is the cutoff we seek.
nodes.statement_short: For a corner starting point, define $\alpha$ on the circumscribed circle times directions, constant along lines, and restrict to $\Gamma_-(\partial\Omega)$.

nodes.name: Regularized operator $I_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$
Regularized operator
nodes.statement: I_{\sigma,E,\alpha} := \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\alpha}}\alpha_{k} I_{\sigma,E}.

nodes.name: Normal operator $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$
Normal operator as sum over cutoffs
nodes.statement: N_{\sigma, E, \alpha} := I_{\sigma, E,\alpha}^{*} I_{\sigma, E, \alpha} =  \sum_{k_{1}=1,k_{2}=1}^{N_{\alpha}}I_{\sigma,E}^{*}\alpha_{k_{1}}\alpha_{k_{2}}I_{\sigma, E}.

nodes.name: Microlocally visible set $\mathcal{M}'$
Microlocally visible set formula
nodes.statement: \mathcal{M}' := \{ (z,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega \, | \, (z,\xi) \in N^{*}\gamma_{x,\theta} \textrm{ for some }(x,\theta) \textrm{ with }\alpha(x,\theta) > 0\}.

nodes.name: Why a reflection threshold is needed
nodes.statement: One reason we need to impose an upper bound on the number of reflections is that as $N$ increases, the open level sets of $N(x,\theta)$ shrink in measure to zero. Similarly, the neighborhoods in $\Gamma_{-}$ on which we have constant reflection signature $(l_{1},l_{2})$ become infinitesimal as $|l_{1}|+|l_{2}| \to \infty$. Thus $\alpha$ will not be smooth unless we apply some threshold.
nodes.statement_short: Level sets of $N$ and constant-signature neighborhoods shrink as reflections grow, so $\alpha$ needs a threshold to be smooth.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement:
We need to construct coordinates near the broken ray $\gamma_{0}$. To do this, we let $\{x_{0,1},\ldots, x_{0,N}\}$ be the ordered reflection points on $\partial \Omega$ for $\gamma_{0}$, where $N = N(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$. We then construct a new domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ consisting of $N$ reflected copies of $\Omega$ which are glued together with the original $\Omega$ along the edges that contain each $x_{0,j}$, $1 \leq j \leq N$. Specifically, let $P_{m}= \{x \in \rn{2} \, | \, (x-x_{0,j}) \cdot \xi_{j} = 0\}$ for $1 \leq j \leq N$ be the hyperplanes in $\rn{2}$ corresponding to the reflection points of $\gamma_{0}$. We iteratively construct $\widetilde{\Omega}$ by starting with $x_{0,1}$ and reflecting $\Omega$ across the hyperplane $P_{1}$. Then glue the two copies of $\Omega$ together along $P_{1}$. Also reflect each hyperplane $P_{j}$ across $P_{1}$ for $2 \leq j \leq N$. Now we consider the reflected hyperplane $P_{2}$, which we still denote with the same notation, and reflect the previously reflected copy of $\Omega$ across it. Continuing in this way, we obtain a space consisting of $N+1$ copies of $\Omega$, each reflected along a specific edge. If $\gamma_{0}$ contains a corner point, we can add additional reflected copies of $\Omega$ as necessary to accommodate nearby broken rays. We also obtain a distribution $\widetilde{f} \in \mathcal{E}'(\widetilde{\Omega})$ and an unfolded version of $\gamma_{0}$, denoted by $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$, using the same process. Note that by reversing the reflection sequence, any covector $(\widetilde{z}, \widetilde{\xi}) \in T^{*}\widetilde{\Omega}$ corresponds to a unique covector $(z,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega$.

Since the edges of $\Omega$ are flat, it follows that $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$ is a straight line. The openness of $E$ and the assumptions on $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ ensure that for $(x,\theta)$ in a neighborhood $V \subset \Gamma_{-}(E)$ of $(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$, the unfolded paths $\widetilde{\gamma}_{x,\theta}$ lie in the same extended space $\widetilde{\Omega}$ and avoid $\partial E$. Now choose a point $p_{0}$ on the line $x_{0} + t\theta_{0}$ for $t < 0$ so that $p_{0} \notin \widetilde{\Omega}$. Define $x = p_{0} + t\theta$. Then $(\theta, t)$ are local coordinates near any point of $\widetilde{\Omega} \cap \widetilde{\gamma}_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$. We can assume without loss of generality that $\theta_{0} = (0,1)$. Writing $x = (x^{1},x^{2}) = (\theta^{1}, t)$, we have the coordinates
\begin{equation*}
U = \{x = (\theta^{1}, t) \, | \, |\theta^{1}| < \epsilon, \, l^{-} < t < l^{+} \} \subset \widetilde{\Omega}.
\end{equation*}
Since $f$ is compactly supported inside of $\Omega$, we may shrink $\epsilon$ as necessary so that we can take $l^{-}, l^{+}$ to be constant. Now as in the proof of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric}, we let $(z_{0}, \xi_{0} )\in N^{*}\gamma_{0}$. Then consider the corresponding reflected covector via path unfolding given by $(\widetilde{z}^{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \in N^{*}\widetilde{\gamma}_{0}$. That is, let $\{\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\ldots, \xi_{m}\}$ the sequence of normal vectors corresponding to the ordered reflection points of the path $\gamma_{0}$ up until reaching the point $z_{0}$. Let $R_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ be the reflection operators across each affine hyperplane $z \cdot \xi_{j} = x_{0,j} \cdot \xi_{j}$ for $1 \leq j \leq m$. Specifically, $R_{j}v = v- 2((v-x_{0,j})\cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{z}_{0} = Rz_{0} := R_{1}R_{2} \cdots R_{m}z_{0}$. Also, consider the operators $A_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ defined as reflections across the hyperplanes $z \cdot \xi_{j} = 0$ that pass through the origin. Specifically, $A_{j}v = v - 2(v \cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{\xi}_{0} = A\xi_{0} := A_{1}A_{2} \cdots A_{m_{z_{0}}}\xi_{0}$. The argument of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric} shows that $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(\widetilde{f})$. 

Now we undo the reflection process to conclude that $(z_{0}, \xi_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$. In particular, we use the respective inverse transformations $A^{-1}$ and $R^{-1}$, generated by $A_{j}^{-1} = A_{j}$ and $R_{j}^{-1} = R_{j}$ to recover $(z_{0},\xi_{0})$ from $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0})$. Note that the reflections $A_{j}, R_{j}$ preserve the singularities of $f$, and so the analytic wavefront set of $\widetilde{f}$ transforms in the obvious way. Thus $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) = (Rz_{0}, A\xi_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(\widetilde{f}) \Longrightarrow (z_{0}, \xi_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$.

nodes.name: Proof that corner reflections reverse direction
nodes.statement: To see this, let $x\in \Omega$ and let $c$ be a corner point. Define $\theta_{c}$ as the angle between $c-x$ and the horizontal axis. For $\theta$ close to $\theta_{c}$, the broken ray from $x$ in the direction $\widehat{\theta}$ will intersect twice near $c$ and return at an angle $\pi+\theta$ with the positive horizontal direction (i.e. it will return in the direction $-\widehat{\theta}$). Therefore, the limit of such rays shows that $\gamma_{x,\theta_{c}}$ unambiguously reflects back towards $x$. This is also consistent with what one expects from path unfolding.
nodes.statement_short: Nearby rays hit both edges near the corner and return in direction $-\hat\theta$; take the limit.

nodes.name: At most two corner points on a regular broken ray

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with two distinct corner points. Since reflections from corners return in the opposite direction from the direction of incidence, any broken ray between them will repeat periodically. Thus, either one of the corner points lies in $E$, or there is a point along the broken ray between them that lies in $E$. But this implies the broken ray would have terminated before hitting both corners.
nodes.statement_short: Between two corners the ray retraces itself periodically, so it would hit $E$ first.

N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f(x) & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta))\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& +  \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta))\, dt \,d\theta. \end{align}
Again suppose that the broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ intersects a corner $c$ at the $m$th reflection, where $1 \leq m \leq N-1$. We claim that in the first summation above, the terms with $j_{2} = m$ vanish. To see this, note that if $(x,\theta)$ is such that $z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta)$ is in the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}$, then reflecting $j_{2} = m$ times from that point will put us in the small ``bow-tie" region near $c$ on which the corresponding line integral vanishes. So we rewrite the first term in (\ref{eq:normalreflectcorner1}) as
\begin{align}
 & \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}, j_{2}\neq m}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta))\, dt \,d\theta. \end{align}
The important thing is that in (\ref{eq:normalreflectcorner2}) the reflection signature of $z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}$ relative to $z_{-j_{1}}$ for each pair $(j_{1},j_{2})$ is the same wherever $\alpha^{2}(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})$ is supported. 

As in \S \ref{sec:normalsimplify}, for each pair of indices $(j_{1},j_{2})$, we consider the reflection signature when going from $(x,\theta)$ to $(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}, \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}})$. This is given by $(h_{j_{2}}- h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})$. So as in (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) we define
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} & = R_{(h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})}(y)\\
\widehat{\eta} & = \frac{1}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}-x|}( (-1)^{h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}}(\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}^{1}- x^{1}), (-1)^{v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}}}(\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}^{2} - x^{2}))\\
\widehat{\theta} & = \frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|},
\end{align*}
and we can rewrite
\begin{align}
 & N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f(x) \notag\\
 & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}\left[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}\right] \left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right)\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\notag\\
& +  \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}]\left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right)\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\notag\\
 & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}\left| \alpha \left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right) \right|^{2}\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|} .
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Terms reflecting into the corner bow-tie vanish; the rest have fixed signatures and, with $q_j$ and $w_{reg,j}$, take the smooth-kernel form (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna}).

assumptions: Under the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:stabilityestimate}, without assuming that $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}$ is injective
conclusions: $\mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}}$ is finite dimensional and included in $C^{\infty}(K)$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement_short: Parametrix gives $QN f = f + S_2 f$ with smoothing $S_2$; elliptic regularity yields (a), Fredholm theory and smoothing yield (b).

nodes.name: $C^k$ estimate of kernel elements
nodes.statement: \|f\|_{C^{k}(K)}= \|S_{2}f\|_{C^{k}(K)} \lesssim \mathrm{sup}_{y\in \Omega}\left( \|S_{2}(\cdot, y)\|_{C^{k}(K)} \right) \|f\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}.

assumptions: Assume that $\sigma, \alpha$ are fixed and belong to $C^{2}$
Let $(\sigma', \alpha')$ be $O(\delta)$ close to $(\sigma, \alpha)$ in $C^{2}$
nodes.statement_short: $C^2$-small perturbations of $(\sigma,\alpha)$ change $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha}$ by $O(\delta)$ as an $L^2(K)\to H^1$ operator.

nodes.statement_short: Ballistic part by the perturbation argument of Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann; reflected kernels depend smoothly on $(\sigma,\alpha)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Broken ray transform on higher-dimensional polyhedral domains
nodes.statement: It is perhaps of interest to carry out similar computations for the broken ray transform on higher dimensional polyhedral domains, or domains where $\partial \Omega \setminus E$ is flat.

nodes.name: Microlocal results for the unit ball
nodes.statement: One interesting problem to consider would be to try to get analogous microlocal results for the unit ball.

nodes.name: Goal: coordinates near the broken ray
nodes.statement: We need to construct coordinates near the broken ray $\gamma_{0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: State the aim: build coordinates near $\gamma_0$.

nodes.name: Construct the unfolded domain
nodes.statement: To do this, we let $\{x_{0,1},\ldots, x_{0,N}\}$ be the ordered reflection points on $\partial \Omega$ for $\gamma_{0}$, where $N = N(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$. We then construct a new domain $\widetilde{\Omega}$ consisting of $N$ reflected copies of $\Omega$ which are glued together with the original $\Omega$ along the edges that contain each $x_{0,j}$, $1 \leq j \leq N$. Specifically, let $P_{m}= \{x \in \rn{2} \, | \, (x-x_{0,j}) \cdot \xi_{j} = 0\}$ for $1 \leq j \leq N$ be the hyperplanes in $\rn{2}$ corresponding to the reflection points of $\gamma_{0}$. We iteratively construct $\widetilde{\Omega}$ by starting with $x_{0,1}$ and reflecting $\Omega$ across the hyperplane $P_{1}$. Then glue the two copies of $\Omega$ together along $P_{1}$. Also reflect each hyperplane $P_{j}$ across $P_{1}$ for $2 \leq j \leq N$. Now we consider the reflected hyperplane $P_{2}$, which we still denote with the same notation, and reflect the previously reflected copy of $\Omega$ across it. Continuing in this way, we obtain a space consisting of $N+1$ copies of $\Omega$, each reflected along a specific edge.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Build $\widetilde\Omega$ by successively reflecting $\Omega$ across the hit edges.

nodes.name: Corners and unfolded objects
nodes.statement: If $\gamma_{0}$ contains a corner point, we can add additional reflected copies of $\Omega$ as necessary to accommodate nearby broken rays. We also obtain a distribution $\widetilde{f} \in \mathcal{E}'(\widetilde{\Omega})$ and an unfolded version of $\gamma_{0}$, denoted by $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$, using the same process. Note that by reversing the reflection sequence, any covector $(\widetilde{z}, \widetilde{\xi}) \in T^{*}\widetilde{\Omega}$ corresponds to a unique covector $(z,\xi) \in T^{*}\Omega$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Unfold $f$ and $\gamma_0$; covectors correspond one-to-one.

nodes.name: Unfolded ray is a straight line
nodes.statement: Since the edges of $\Omega$ are flat, it follows that $\widetilde{\gamma_{0}}$ is a straight line. The openness of $E$ and the assumptions on $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ ensure that for $(x,\theta)$ in a neighborhood $V \subset \Gamma_{-}(E)$ of $(x_{0}, \theta_{0})$, the unfolded paths $\widetilde{\gamma}_{x,\theta}$ lie in the same extended space $\widetilde{\Omega}$ and avoid $\partial E$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Flat edges make the unfolded rays straight lines in a common $\widetilde\Omega$.

nodes.name: Local coordinates
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Introduce coordinates $(\theta^1,t)$ around the unfolded ray.

nodes.name: Reflect the covector
nodes.statement: Now as in the proof of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric}, we let $(z_{0}, \xi_{0} )\in N^{*}\gamma_{0}$. Then consider the corresponding reflected covector via path unfolding given by $(\widetilde{z}^{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \in N^{*}\widetilde{\gamma}_{0}$. That is, let $\{\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\ldots, \xi_{m}\}$ the sequence of normal vectors corresponding to the ordered reflection points of the path $\gamma_{0}$ up until reaching the point $z_{0}$. Let $R_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ be the reflection operators across each affine hyperplane $z \cdot \xi_{j} = x_{0,j} \cdot \xi_{j}$ for $1 \leq j \leq m$. Specifically, $R_{j}v = v- 2((v-x_{0,j})\cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{z}_{0} = Rz_{0} := R_{1}R_{2} \cdots R_{m}z_{0}$. Also, consider the operators $A_{j}:\rn{2} \to \rn{2}$ defined as reflections across the hyperplanes $z \cdot \xi_{j} = 0$ that pass through the origin. Specifically, $A_{j}v = v - 2(v \cdot \xi_{j})\xi_{j}$. We then define $\widetilde{\xi}_{0} = A\xi_{0} := A_{1}A_{2} \cdots A_{m_{z_{0}}}\xi_{0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Map $(z_0,\xi_0)$ to the unfolded covector via reflections $R$ and $A$.

nodes.name: Apply the X-ray microlocal argument
nodes.statement: The argument of Proposition 1 in \cite{xraygeneric} shows that $(\widetilde{z}_{0}, \widetilde{\xi}_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(\widetilde{f})$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 1 of Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann on $\widetilde\Omega$.

nodes.name: Undo the reflections
nodes.statement: Now we undo the reflection process to conclude that $(z_{0}, \xi_{0}) \notin \mathrm{WF}_{A}(f)$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Reflections preserve analytic singularities, so $(z_0,\xi_0)\notin\mathrm{WF}_A(f)$.

nodes.name: Analyticity from Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Suppose $I_{\sigma, E}f = 0$. By Proposition \ref{thm:microlocalsquare} we have that $f$ is analytic on $K$.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 1 gives analyticity of $f$ on $K$.

nodes.name: Entire and zero
nodes.statement: Since $\mathrm{supp}(f) \subset K$, we have that $f$ can be extended to an entire function and hence must be identically zero.
nodes.section: 3 Injectivity of $I_{0, E}$ for the Square
nodes.statement_short: Compact support makes $f$ entire, hence zero.

nodes.name: Choose cutoff and write the pairing
nodes.statement_short: Fix a cutoff with constant reflection count and write the adjoint pairing.

nodes.name: Change of variables
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $(y,\eta)=(z_j+t\theta_j,\theta_j)$ and track the shifted indices.

nodes.name: Diffeomorphism and Jacobian
nodes.statement_short: The substitution is a diffeomorphism onto $\Omega\times\mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ with Jacobian factor $J_j$.

nodes.name: Jacobian equals one
nodes.statement: Since the billiard map $T$ preserves the symplectic form $|\nu(x) \cdot \theta| dx \wedge d\theta$ on $\Gamma_{-}$, it follows that $J_{j}(y,\eta) = 1$. We stress that this is even true for domains with piecewise smooth boundary as is the case for the square, by measure theoretic arguments (see \cite{serge2} \S 1.7). One can verify that the Jacobian factors above cancel by first making the change of variables $(x,\theta)\to T^{j}(x,\theta)$ in (\ref{eq:adjointcomputation}), using the invariance of the symplectic form $|\nu(x)\cdot \theta| dx\wedge d\theta$ under $T$. Then change to $(y,\eta)$ coordinates on $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ using the same approach as in (Theorem 1 (b), \cite{inversesource}).
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of the symplectic form under $T$ gives $J_j=1$.

nodes.name: Signatures and notation
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the signature sequence, unfolded hit point $\widetilde z$ and notation.

nodes.name: Equations for the hit point
nodes.statement_short: Write $\widetilde z$ for a top or right edge hit.

nodes.name: Angle substitution
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $\eta=S_{l_1,l_2}(\theta)$ and express $z(x,\eta)$.

nodes.name: Jacobian of the position substitution
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $y=z+t\hat\eta$ and compute its Jacobian.

nodes.name: Express $z$ via $x,y$
nodes.statement_short: Solve for the hit point using the reflection law.

nodes.name: Jacobian simplifies to $|\widetilde y-x|$
nodes.statement_short: The Jacobian is $|\widetilde y-x|$, bounded below for nonzero signatures.

nodes.name: Reflected term formula
nodes.statement_short: Each reflected term is an integral with kernel over $|\widetilde y-x|$.

nodes.name: Smoothness of the cutoff factor
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\alpha_k\circ T^{-j_2}$ by a smooth expression through $q_j$.

nodes.name: Smoothness of the weights
nodes.statement: We observe that the definitions of $w_{j_{1}}, w_{j_{2}}$ also involve $\tau_{-}$, which is not smooth on $\Omega \times \mathbb{S}^{1}$. However, since $\sigma$ is compactly supported inside of $\Omega$ on some smooth subdomain, we can modify $\tau_{-}$ inside of $w_{j_{1}},w_{j_{2}}$ as necessary to be smooth without changing the integrals. In particular, we can use the functions $q_{j}$ to define the weight functions instead of the billiard map $T$ and boundary distance function $\tau_{-}$.
nodes.statement_short: Modify $\tau_-$ inside the weights using $q_j$ so they are smooth.

nodes.name: Fix point and corner
nodes.statement: To see this, let $x\in \Omega$ and let $c$ be a corner point. Define $\theta_{c}$ as the angle between $c-x$ and the horizontal axis.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $x$, a corner $c$ and the angle $\theta_c$.

nodes.name: Nearby rays reverse
nodes.statement: For $\theta$ close to $\theta_{c}$, the broken ray from $x$ in the direction $\widehat{\theta}$ will intersect twice near $c$ and return at an angle $\pi+\theta$ with the positive horizontal direction (i.e. it will return in the direction $-\widehat{\theta}$).
nodes.statement_short: Nearby rays return in the opposite direction.

nodes.name: Limit
nodes.statement: Therefore, the limit of such rays shows that $\gamma_{x,\theta_{c}}$ unambiguously reflects back towards $x$. This is also consistent with what one expects from path unfolding.
nodes.statement_short: The limiting corner ray reflects back toward $x$.

nodes.name: Two corners give periodic ray
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ with two distinct corner points. Since reflections from corners return in the opposite direction from the direction of incidence, any broken ray between them will repeat periodically.
nodes.statement_short: Assume two corners; the ray between them is periodic.

nodes.name: A point in $E$
nodes.statement: Thus, either one of the corner points lies in $E$, or there is a point along the broken ray between them that lies in $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Some corner or intermediate point lies in $E$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: But this implies the broken ray would have terminated before hitting both corners.
nodes.statement_short: The ray would have terminated earlier.

nodes.name: Corner notation
nodes.statement: We will use $c \neq x_{0}$ to refer to a corner in the broken ray if it has one, and we will allow for the possibility that $x_{0}$ itself is a corner point. However, as previously discussed, $x_{0}$ being a corner point does not present any problem with regard to the smoothness of the integrands involved in the expansion of the localized normal operator (see the discussion following (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm})). As before, let $K \Subset \Omega$ be the set on which we assume $f$ has support.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for the corner and support $K$; corner starting points pose no problem.

nodes.name: Neighborhood of rays near the corner
nodes.statement: So given our broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$, we assume it passes through a corner point $c \neq x_{0}$ at the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection, where $1 \leq m \leq N-1$, and $N-1$ is the total number of reflections of the curve. Choose a neighborhood $U$ consisting of $(x,\theta) \in \Gamma_{-}(E)$ that are sufficiently close to $(x_{0},\theta_{0})$ in the following sense. At the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection, most nearby broken rays to $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ will undergo a reflection along a very short segment near the corner on which $f$ vanishes and $\sigma = 0$. In particular, such segments do not affect the weights $w_{j}$ and so we will be able to discard them. Thus, we choose $U$ small enough so that at the $m$th reflection, all nearby broken rays to $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ either pass through the corner $c$ or hit close enough to the corner so as to reflect into a short path that contributes nothing to the integral. Note that for such broken rays from $U$ passing very near to the corner $c$ (but not actually touching it), after the $(m+1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ reflection they will be oriented in a direction opposite their respective directions during the $(m-1)^{\mathrm{th}}$ segment. We also choose $U$ small enough so as not to introduce any new corner points among the included broken rays.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $U$ so rays near the corner either hit it or contribute nothing.

nodes.name: Indicator and split transform
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\mathbbm{1}_U$ and split the localized transform.

nodes.name: Adjoint and normal operator
nodes.statement_short: Compute the adjoint and normal operator of the split transform.

nodes.name: Ballistic terms
nodes.statement:
Then break off the part with $j_{2} = j_{1}$ to obtain
\begin{align*}
N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) & =  \sum_{j=0}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& +  \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta + t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta.\notag.
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Isolate the ballistic terms $j_1=j_2$.

nodes.name: Drop bow-tie term and combine
nodes.statement:
Now we have to be a bit careful in order to combine both summands. In the first summand, whenever $(z_{-m}(x,\theta), \theta_{-m}(x,\theta))$ is in the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})\alpha^{2}$, we know that $x+\tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta + t\theta$ is a line segment very near the corner $c$ where $f$ vanishes. Thus we can throw out the term involving $j = m$. Now for the terms with $j < m$, we may immediately combine the summands into one, thus eliminating the presence of $\mathbbm{1}_{U}$. That is, we have
\begin{align}
N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) & = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(z_{-j}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& + \sum_{j_{1}=m+1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{1}}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& + \sum_{j_{2}=m}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{2}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{2}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{2}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta + t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Discard the vanishing $j=m$ term and merge the $j<m$ summands.

nodes.name: Matching signatures and regularized weights
nodes.statement_short: Shifted indices share the same signature; define regularized weights $w_{reg,j}$ via $q_m$.

nodes.name: Rewrite the ballistic part
nodes.statement:
This allows us to rewrite the ballistic part of the normal operator as
\begin{align*}
& N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}f(x) \\
& = \sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(z_{-j}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j}(x,\theta))w_{j}(x,\theta)  [w_{j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& + \sum_{j=m}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}|\alpha|^{2}(q_{j}(x,\theta), S_{h_{j}, v_{j}}^{-1}(\theta))w_{reg,j}(x,\theta) [w_{reg,j}f](x + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)\theta+ t\theta, \theta)\, dt \,d\theta \notag.
\end{align*}
From here, we can make the change of variables $s = t + \tau_{-}(x,\theta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with $w_{reg,j}$ and shift $s=t+\tau_-$.

nodes.name: Recall reflected part
nodes.statement:
Now we need to deal with $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$. However, the approach is similar. Recall we have
\begin{align}
N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f(x) & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta))\, dt \,d\theta \notag\\
& +  \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{1}}\int_{\rn{+}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}](z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta))w_{j_{1}}(x,\theta) \notag\\
& \quad \cdot [w_{j_{2}}f](z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta) + t\theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta), \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}}(x,\theta))\, dt \,d\theta. \end{align}
Again suppose that the broken ray $\gamma_{x_{0},\theta_{0}}$ intersects a corner $c$ at the $m$th reflection, where $1 \leq m \leq N-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the reflected part with corner and the corner at reflection $m$.

nodes.name: Terms with $j_2=m$ vanish
nodes.statement_short: Claim and show the $j_2=m$ terms vanish, then rewrite.

nodes.name: Bow-tie argument
nodes.statement: To see this, note that if $(x,\theta)$ is such that $z_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta),\theta_{-j_{1}}(x,\theta)$ is in the support of $(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}$, then reflecting $j_{2} = m$ times from that point will put us in the small ``bow-tie" region near $c$ on which the corresponding line integral vanishes.
nodes.statement_short: Reflecting $m$ times lands in the bow-tie where line integrals vanish.

nodes.name: Rewrite first term
nodes.statement_short: Drop the $j_2=m$ terms.

nodes.name: Constant signatures
nodes.statement: The important thing is that in (\ref{eq:normalreflectcorner2}) the reflection signature of $z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}$ relative to $z_{-j_{1}}$ for each pair $(j_{1},j_{2})$ is the same wherever $\alpha^{2}(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})$ is supported.
nodes.statement_short: Each index pair has a fixed reflection signature on the support.

nodes.name: Smooth-kernel form
nodes.statement:
As in \S \ref{sec:normalsimplify}, for each pair of indices $(j_{1},j_{2})$, we consider the reflection signature when going from $(x,\theta)$ to $(z_{j_{2}-j_{1}}, \theta_{j_{2}-j_{1}})$. This is given by $(h_{j_{2}}- h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})$. So as in (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) we define
\begin{align*}
\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} & = R_{(h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}, v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}})}(y)\\
\widehat{\eta} & = \frac{1}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}-x|}( (-1)^{h_{j_{2}}-h_{j_{1}}}(\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}^{1}- x^{1}), (-1)^{v_{j_{2}}-v_{j_{1}}}(\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}}^{2} - x^{2}))\\
\widehat{\theta} & = \frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|},
\end{align*}
and we can rewrite
\begin{align}
 & N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f(x) \notag\\
 & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}\left[(1-\mathbbm{1}_{U})|\alpha|^{2}\right] \left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right)\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\notag\\
& +  \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}[\mathbbm{1}_{U}|\alpha|^{2}]\left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right)\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\notag\\
 & = \sum_{j_{1}=0}^{N-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0, j_{2}\neq j_{1}}^{N-1}\int_{\rn{2}}\left| \alpha \left(q_{j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right), S_{h_{j_{1}},v_{j_{1}}}^{-1}\left(\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right)\right) \right|^{2}\notag\\
 & \quad \cdot w_{reg,j_{1}}\left(x,\frac{\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|}\right) \, w_{reg,j_{2}}(y, \widehat{\eta})\, f(y) \, \frac{dy}{|\widetilde{y}_{j_{1},j_{2}} - x|} .
\end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute as in the corner-free case to reach the smooth-kernel form.

nodes.name: Recall decomposition
nodes.statement_short: Recall the ballistic/reflected decomposition and ellipticity.

nodes.name: Parametrix
nodes.statement: So we have a parametrix $Q$ of $N_{\sigma, E,\alpha, ballistic}$ of order $1$ that is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take an order-1 parametrix $Q$ of the ballistic part.

nodes.name: Reflected part has smooth kernel
nodes.statement: For the reflected part, we have a sum of terms of the form (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) in the case of a neighborhood of broken rays that don't have any corner points (except possibly as a starting point), or $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ has the form of (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna}), both of which have $C_{0}^{\infty}$ Schwartz kernels.
nodes.statement_short: Both reflected forms have $C_0^\infty$ kernels.

nodes.name: Apply $Q$
nodes.statement: Applying $Q$ to both sides of (\ref{eq:normalop}) yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $Q$ to the decomposition.

nodes.name: Same as FSU Proposition 3
nodes.statement: The proof is essentially the same as that for (\cite{xraygeneric}, Proposition 3).
nodes.statement_short: The proof follows Proposition 3 of Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement_short: Parametrix identity plus elliptic regularity give the a priori estimate.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement_short: Kernel elements solve $(\mathrm{Id}+S_2)f=0$, are smooth, and form a finite-dimensional space.

nodes.name: Kernel equation
nodes.statement: For part (b), if $f \in \mathrm{Ker}{\, I_{\sigma, E, \alpha} }$, then $(\mathrm{Id} + S_{2})f = 0$, and also $S_{2}$ is a compact operator on $L^{2}(K)$ with smooth Schwartz kernel. Clearly $S_{2}f \in L^{2}$ if $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\Omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel elements satisfy $(\mathrm{Id}+S_2)f=0$ with compact $S_2$.

nodes.name: Smoothness
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $C^k$ norms through the smooth kernel of $S_2$.

nodes.name: Finite dimension
nodes.statement: Finally, the fact that $I+S_{2}$ is Fredholm implies that its kernel is finite dimensional.
nodes.statement_short: Fredholmness gives a finite-dimensional kernel.

nodes.name: Recall decomposition
nodes.statement: Recall that $N_{\sigma,E,\alpha} = N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic} + N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$, where $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is a weakly singular integral operator with smooth kernel and $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is smoothing.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the ballistic/reflected decomposition.

nodes.name: Ballistic perturbation
nodes.statement_short: Perturbation bound for the ballistic part from Frigyik-Stefanov-Uhlmann.

nodes.name: Reflected perturbation
nodes.statement: Similarly, the Schwartz kernels of $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ depend smoothly on $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ (see (\ref{eq:normalreflectedterm}) and (\ref{eq:normalreflectbigkahuna})), so the same estimate holds for this term. The completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Reflected kernels depend smoothly on $(\sigma,\alpha)$, giving the same bound.

nodes.name: Injectivity of $N$
nodes.statement: First note that if $I_{\sigma, E, \alpha}: L^{2}(K) \to L^{2}(\Gamma_{-})$ is injective, then $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha}:L^{2}(K)\to H^{1}(\Omega)$ is also injective by an integration by parts.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of $I$ implies injectivity of $N$.

nodes.name: Parametrix and compact remainder
nodes.statement: Next, since $N_{\sigma, E, \alpha, ballistic}$ is elliptic on $\mathcal{M}$, we may apply a parametrix $Q$ to get the equation $QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha}f = f + S_{1}f + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}f$. Note that $S_{1} + QN_{\sigma, E, \alpha, reflect}$ is compact.
nodes.statement_short: Apply a parametrix; the remainder is compact.

nodes.name: Elliptic regularity estimate
nodes.statement_short: Elliptic regularity gives an estimate with a compact error term.

nodes.name: Remove compact term
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2 of Stefanov removes the compact term using injectivity.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4 transfers the estimate to nearby $(\sigma,\alpha)$.
